triplets.tail: Recession of 1969–1970: GDP growth slowed, unemployment rose to 6%, tight monetary policy raised interest rates

triplets.head: Unocal / Moran / Revlon trilogy

triplets.head: Sarbanes-Oxley Act
triplets.tail: Post-Enron/WorldCom governance reform; increased compliance costs

triplets.head: Dodd-Frank Act
triplets.tail: Post-GFC financial regulation; Volcker Rule; SIFI oversight; restricted proprietary trading and derivatives

triplets.head: Basel III
triplets.tail: Higher bank capital requirements; increased cost of leveraged lending

triplets.head: Merger wave termination pattern
triplets.tail: Every wave ended through combination of: (a) financial/economic shock disrupting financing mechanism, (b) deal failures revealing limits of dominant thesis, (c) regulatory response raising barriers to future deal-making

triplets.head: Merger wave drivers
triplets.tail: Real economic shocks (technology, deregulation) trigger waves; requires sufficient capital liquidity

triplets.head: Merger wave drivers
triplets.tail: Stock overvaluation and managerial irrationality drive waves; markets inefficient

triplets.head: Merger wave drivers
triplets.tail: Both forces operate simultaneously — waves require both economic shock AND capital liquidity

triplets.head: Merger wave financing
triplets.tail: The financing innovation that enabled each wave also contained the seeds of its destruction; each wave pushed its financing mechanism to excess, creating fragility

triplets.head: Agency cycle in M&A
triplets.tail: Build-Up (managers exploit agency slack) → Correction (market for corporate control activates) → Defense (managers entrench via poison pills, anti-takeover laws) → New Cycle

triplets.head: Agency-based M&A theory
triplets.tail: Shleifer & Vishny (2003) — bridges agency and behavioral traditions, explains wave timing and predicts medium of payment (stock vs. cash)
